children: A U.S. federal judge has allowed Connecticut firefighters to pursue claims against more than 20 companies, including 3M
, alleging that chemicals in protective gear exposed them to toxic "forever chemicals" and increased their cancer risk.

U.S. District Judge Alvin Thompson in Hartford, Connecticut, ruled Tuesday that 13 firefighter unions and 12 individual firefighters had sufficient grounds to seek damages and medical monitoring, even when they had no outward symptoms of cancer or other diseases.

The plaintiffs allege that PFAS in protective "turnout gear" can enter the body through skin absorption, ingestion, and inhalation. Their lawyers have described the case as the first proposed class action focused exclusively on firefighter equipment containing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS.
Thompson also found that the plaintiffs had adequately alleged that 3M
had a duty to warn about the risks associated with the chemicals and had acted negligently.
Kevlar were among the PFAS-containing components used in firefighters’ protective gear, while Honeywell
manufactured the turnout gear. Some liabilities associated with DuPont
The companies have sought to have the claims dismissed. 3M

argued there were no plausible allegations connecting Scotchlite to the firefighters’ gear, while other defendants disputed claims that the equipment failed to protect firefighters from fire-related hazards.
The lawsuit was filed in June 2024.
